claims.claim: Some Nippur temple-linked rights were specified as recurring periods within a year, rather than undifferentiated full-time offices.
claims.date: Samsuiluna 11–12 in the directly dated core
claims.context: Martu/Kusu transactions; no secure household loci
claims.primary: G-I01–02: BE 6/2 36 and 39. G-I09 is lower-resolution corroboration.
claims.secondary: Poebel’s functional glosses are not required to establish the written annual periods.
claims.counter: Annual periods do not prove exact days worked, a universal rota, or the same calendar in all texts.
claims.limit: The particular rights described, not every Nippur institution.
claims.relevance: Separates a family-held entitlement from a presumed lifetime occupation.

claims.claim: The selected Nippur corpus attests both sale and exchange of temple-office rights.
claims.secondary: S04 abstract identifies the topic, but is not evidentiary support for the individual transactions.
claims.counter: No proof that all offices were freely alienable or that no eligibility/approval conditions existed.
claims.limit: Documented conveyances, not an unrestricted citywide market regime.
claims.relevance: Institutional connection could change through transactions as well as kinship.

claims.claim: Office-linked rights could form part of family patrimony alongside other assets, without all family property necessarily merging.
claims.context: Inherited Martu rights, paternal recovery, adoption and estate division
claims.primary: G-I01, G-I04, G-I08; G-I10 supplies catalogue-level corroboration.
claims.secondary: Archive-scale strategies are a further reconstruction, not directly stated.
claims.counter: A shared father does not prove co-residence; inheritance is not equivalent to inalienability.
claims.limit: Named property-holding cases; no prevalence estimate.
claims.relevance: Links institutional resources to durable family histories.

claims.claim: Two exchanges balance unequal office/land packages with silver, demonstrating negotiated equivalence in those transactions.
claims.primary: G-I02–03: BE 6/2 39 has 5 shekels; no. 37 has 2 shekels.
claims.counter: Mixed assets, damaged terms and differing temples prevent a standardized price comparison.
claims.limit: Two transaction-specific adjustments; not annual earnings or a price index.
claims.relevance: Shows connections between office rights, land and liquid resources.

claims.claim: Some Nippur reacquisitions explicitly characterize the recovered resource as belonging to the paternal house.
claims.date: BE 6/2 45 = Samsuiluna 14/12; no. 66 exact date not recovered
claims.context: Office recovery and a titled woman’s land recovery
claims.secondary: Poebel calls these redemptions; a compulsory family redemption rule is not established.
claims.counter: His Biblical analogy cannot supply a Nippur legal rule; causes of the earlier alienations are unknown.
claims.confidence: HIGH for the family-recovery language; MODERATE for legal mechanism
claims.limit: Two deeds and their stated family reference, not all lineage property.
claims.relevance: Continuity may include reacquisition after alienation.

claims.claim: A Nippur adoption deed protects specified office/property rights of the adoptee against claims by the named adoptive brother.
claims.primary: G-I08: BE 6/2 57, property and no-claim clauses.
claims.secondary: Later edition located but not read; identification of every earlier relationship remains provisional.
claims.counter: The deed does not establish that adoption transferred priestly qualification or actual cultic duty.
claims.limit: One explicit contractual arrangement; not a standard motive for all adoption.
claims.relevance: Created kinship and institutional patrimony could be negotiated together.

claims.claim: A woman bearing a Ninurta-related religious title is documented recovering paternal-house land from another similarly titled woman.
claims.primary: G-I07: title, patronymics, field recovery, silver consideration.
claims.secondary: Exact modern interpretation of SAL-ISḪIB is left open.
claims.counter: Religious affiliation does not make the field temple-owned or prove a female prebend sale.
claims.limit: Named titled women; no statement about all women’s access to every office.
claims.relevance: Women’s institutional affiliation and family property action can coexist.

claims.claim: One Ninlil-related family dispute records royal referral to Nippur’s council followed by a house/property settlement.
claims.primary: G-I05: BE 6/2 10, lines 1–36; S12 identifies P259799.
claims.secondary: Poebel’s wider theory of the council is not adopted.
claims.counter: A recorded royal referral is not evidence that every dispute followed this route or that this was a modern appellate hierarchy.
claims.limit: The route documented by this deed and its account of prior proceedings.
claims.relevance: Family-held institutional rights could involve multiple legal authorities.

claims.claim: Receipt of deeds for an office and inheritance after a former holder’s death carried explicit responsibility for future claims.
claims.date: Samsuiluna 13/12; two-year interval in the text
claims.secondary: Poebel infers temple disposition from the witnesses/seals; that inference is kept distinct from the deed’s wording.
claims.counter: Recipient’s kinship, payment, and whether this is a new grant or delivery of pre-existing title are not established.
claims.limit: One documentary transfer; not a universal temple succession procedure.
claims.relevance: Custody, proof and liability were additional interfaces beyond asset transfer.

claims.claim: The core conveyances establish terms and transfers more securely than realized net household income or actual performance of every listed office.
claims.date: Dates of the selected legal cases
claims.primary: G-I01–04, G-I06, G-I08; sale price, adjustment and office designation are distinct observations.
claims.counter: Administrative evidence can record actual allocations, but cannot automatically be merged with unrelated conveyances.
claims.limit: Not a claim that remuneration records never existed or that no prebend was profitable.
claims.relevance: Prevents capital values or administered resources from becoming fictitious household budgets.

claims.claim: Administrative cases add work/allocation relationships not visible in the office-conveyance cases.
claims.date: Late-Rim-Sin dossier; exact calendar conversion unresolved
claims.type: Published primary edition/table via specialist study
claims.secondary: Archival identification follows S03; this report does not reconstruct workers’ households.
claims.counter: Payment entries do not establish permanent employment or social-class membership.
claims.limit: Particular recorded tasks; not a representative non-elite population.
claims.relevance: Broadens the interface beyond office and property holders.

claims.claim: Title, commodity receipt or co-occurrence alone is insufficient to identify a personal household or its hierarchy.
claims.date: Scope rule applied to the late-Rim-Sin administrative cases
claims.primary: The case table records the observed relation, leaving unsupported membership unstated.
claims.secondary: See §4.8 for the precisely bounded Goddeeris/Robertson issue.
claims.counter: Explicit kinship or dependency statements could alter a particular identification; absence here does not disprove a relationship.
claims.confidence: HIGH as an evidentiary restriction, not as an ancient social fact
claims.limit: No verdict about all members or leaders of a reconstructed institution.
claims.relevance: Keeps resource administration distinct from presumed domestic dependence.

claims.claim: This selected documentary corpus cannot supply the prevalence of office holding across Nippur households.
claims.context: Property conveyances plus a small administrative supplement
claims.type: Corpus audit, not an ancient proposition
claims.primary: Selection register and access tiers in §2 and accompanying notes.
claims.secondary: The corpus is deliberately relevance-selected, not a census or random sample.
claims.counter: More cases alone would not create a known household denominator.
claims.limit: No citywide distribution, elite share or gender participation rate.
claims.relevance: Prevents named property holders from becoming a population model.

claims.claim: The present return does not establish a change-rate or a continuous institutional trajectory across 1900–1600 BCE.
claims.date: Approved frame versus actually represented regnal clusters
claims.context: Different periods are represented by different genres and access levels
claims.primary: Timeline in §4.10; dated G-I01, G-I03, G-I09–11 and administrative supplement.
claims.secondary: Political-phase interpretation is not supplied by the order of selected records.
claims.counter: A transaction sequence may show local change without supporting a citywide trend.
claims.limit: Neither stasis nor decline is inferred for unsampled intervals.
claims.relevance: Keeps time-specific interfaces from becoming timeless institutions.

claims.claim: BE 6/2 37 is a plausible but unverified antecedent for the exchange recalled in OBCN I 32.
claims.context: Nuska rights; similarly named Šumum-libši and Lu-Ešumeša
claims.secondary: Proposed by this return as a verification target, not an accepted concordance.
claims.counter: Titles, patronymics, exact asset identity and damaged periods require comparison with full editions.
claims.limit: Do not merge the documents into one asset history yet.
claims.relevance: Potential evidence for multi-stage circulation, conditional on identity checks.

claims.claim: The documented household–institution interfaces are not reducible to a single relationship of family membership.
claims.context: Different temples, actors and legal/documentary processes
claims.type: Analytical synthesis of distinct primary cases
claims.primary: G-I01–08 distinguish sale, family claim, recovery, adoption, legal referral and deed custody.
claims.secondary: This is not a claim that temples lacked households; it limits what these documents themselves establish.
claims.counter: Specific institutional households may exist and require separate evidence.
claims.limit: No organizational chart, universal institution type or residence rule follows.
claims.relevance: Preserves different forms of institutional connection without designing their representation.
